prompt: The shop's budget of 50 reaches 100% of its actual cost on the 25th. What happens to the subscription's resources?
hint: Microsoft's documentation answers in one line.

choices.text: Nothing: they keep running, and keep charging
choices.why: Right. A budget notifies; the consumption isn't stopped.

choices.text: They are deallocated until the month ends
choices.why: Nothing is deallocated by a budget. Deallocating needs an action group and a program you wrote.

choices.text: New resources are refused, existing ones keep running
choices.why: A budget refuses nothing. Refusing a request is what a policy does, lesson 4.

choices.text: The subscription switches to its spending limit
choices.why: A spending limit belongs to some credit offers and exists apart from any budget.

prompt: A monthly budget is 50 and an actual alert is set at 80%. At what cost, in the same currency, does the alert fire?
hint: 80% of the amount.

prompt: On the 3rd of the month, a forgotten machine costing 2 a day has charged 6. Which of the shop's two alerts can already fire, and why?
hint: Project the month.

choices.text: The actual one, since any cost counts against it
choices.why: The actual alert waits for 40 of real charges, which this machine reaches on the 20th.

choices.text: Neither, until the month's first invoice
choices.why: Budgets read cost data daily, not invoices.

choices.text: The forecast one: the month projects to about 60
choices.why: Right. 2 a day for thirty days passes the budget of 50, which is what the forecast compares.

choices.text: Both, since 6 is above 80% of a day's share
choices.why: Budgets compare the month's totals with the month's amount, not with a daily share.

prompt: Which of the two alerts can be wrong, and in which direction?
hint: One reports the past and one projects the future.

choices.text: The actual one, which counts charges that may be refunded later
choices.why: A refund is a new charge in the other direction; what was charged was charged.

choices.text: The forecast one, in either direction
choices.why: Right. An early one-off charge inflates it, and a cost that starts late is invisible to it.

choices.text: Neither: both read the same data
choices.why: Same data, but one of them extrapolates from it, and an extrapolation can miss.

choices.text: The forecast one, but only upwards
choices.why: It misses downwards too: a cost that only begins on the 20th stays out of the projection until then.

prompt: A script creates a large virtual machine by mistake at 9:00 on Monday. Going by Microsoft's documented delays, what is the earliest the budget's e-mail can be counted on?
hint: Data, then evaluation, then e-mail.

choices.text: Within the hour, since alerts are sent within an hour
choices.why: The hour is counted from the evaluation, which waits for the data.

choices.text: At midnight, when every budget is reset
choices.why: Budgets reset at the start of their period, a month here, not daily.

choices.text: Never, since a machine's cost reaches budgets only on the invoice
choices.why: Usage reaches Cost Management within hours, not at invoicing.

choices.text: Not before Tuesday: up to 24 hours of data delay plus a daily evaluation
choices.why: Right. More than a day of head start, which is why the amount is kept small.

prompt: An alert on where the month is heading has the threshold type `___`.
hint: The word Azure stores, not the shop's name for the alert.

prompt: Why must `startDate` in the budget be the first day of a month?
hint: What does a monthly budget count?

choices.text: Forecasts can only be made from the first day onwards
choices.why: The forecast follows from the period, not the other way round.

choices.text: Bicep refuses any date that is not the first
choices.why: The parameter is a string to Bicep; Azure is what holds the rule.

choices.text: The invoice is always issued on the first
choices.why: Some invoices follow a billing period that is not the calendar month; the budget's rule is about its own period.

choices.text: A monthly budget counts whole months, from zero each time
choices.why: Right. The count restarts on the first of each month.

prompt: `typo.bicep` has `thresholdType: 'Forecast'`. What did `az bicep build` do with it?
hint: Read the transcript under the first `sed`.

choices.text: Compiled it silently, as if nothing were wrong
choices.why: Right. The property is a plain string to Bicep, so any string passes.

choices.text: Printed the warning BCP036
choices.why: BCP036 came for the amount written as text, in the second copy.

choices.text: Refused it with an error naming the allowed values
choices.why: That was Terraform. Bicep printed nothing at all.

choices.text: Corrected it to `Forecasted`
choices.why: A compiler that rewrote your values would be worse than one that misses them.

prompt: `az bicep build` printed `Warning BCP036` for `amount: '50'`. Was a template written?
hint: Warning or error?

choices.text: No: any BCP code stops the build
choices.why: Lesson 2's BCP135 was an error and stopped it; this one is a warning.

choices.text: Yes, with the value converted to the number 50
choices.why: Bicep does not convert; it passes on what you wrote.

choices.text: Yes, with the value in it as text
choices.why: Right. A warning still writes the template, which is why warnings must be read.

choices.text: Only after asking Azure whether the type is right
choices.why: Building sends nothing to Azure.

prompt: Why did Terraform refuse `Forecast` when Bicep let it through?
hint: Who writes each tool's knowledge of the field?

choices.text: Terraform asked Azure to check it
choices.why: `validate` sends nothing to Azure; `plan` is where it would ask.

choices.text: Its provider's authors listed the allowed values
choices.why: Right. Hand-written validation knows rules the generated types do not.

choices.text: Terraform is stricter than Bicep in every field
choices.why: Bicep knows every property of every API version; which tool catches a mistake depends on the field.

choices.text: Bicep checks types only when deploying
choices.why: Bicep checked the amount's type at build time, with BCP036.

prompt: The typo was in the second `notification` block, yet Terraform reported `notification.0`. What explains the number?
hint: How does Terraform keep these blocks?

choices.text: The first block also had an error that went unreported
choices.why: After the typo was put back, validation passed: the first block was fine.

choices.text: Terraform validates blocks from the bottom up
choices.why: There is no order to go bottom up in; the blocks are an unordered set.

choices.text: Terraform keeps the blocks as a set, with no order
choices.why: Right. A set has no first or second, so the index in the message says nothing about the file.

choices.text: Azure numbers notifications from zero when it stores them
choices.why: Nothing reached Azure; the number is Terraform's own.

prompt: What does it take to make a budget stop machines, rather than only send e-mail?
hint: A budget can call something.

choices.text: An action group that runs something you wrote, such as a runbook
choices.why: Right, at the scope of a subscription or a resource group. The brake is your program.

choices.text: Placing it at the scope of a management group
choices.why: At that scope a budget cannot call an action group at all.

choices.text: Setting its threshold above 100%
choices.why: Thresholds up to 1000% are allowed and every one of them only notifies.

choices.text: Changing `category` from `Cost` to `Usage`
choices.why: The category says what is counted, not what happens when it is crossed.

prompt: Match each mistake to what the lab did with it.
hint: Three answers came back; one mistake never reached a tool.

prompt: A developer with a role on one resource group opens cost analysis and sees a small monthly total. What has she most likely seen?
hint: What decides what a view contains?

choices.text: The company's total, since cost analysis ignores roles
choices.why: You see only the scopes you hold a role on.

choices.text: Only her resource group's cost
choices.why: Right. The scope is the first choice of every view, and hers is one group.

choices.text: Yesterday's cost only, because of the data delay
choices.why: The delay leaves out the last hours, not the rest of the month.

choices.text: The amortised cost, which is always smaller
choices.why: Amortised moves costs between days; over a month it is not systematically smaller.

prompt: The forecast alert has fired. Put the questions to ask cost analysis in the lesson's order.
hint: From when, to what kind, to which one, to who.
items: show the month's daily costs and find the step
group by resource, filtered to that service
read the resource's activity log for who changed it
trap: The activity log comes last: it answers who, and only once you know which resource to ask about.

prompt: A machine left on costs a small, steady amount every day. Which alarm catches it, a budget or an anomaly alert?
hint: What does each one compare against?

choices.text: The anomaly alert, which is built for forgotten resources
choices.why: A steady cost becomes the subscription's pattern, so it never looks anomalous.

choices.text: Both equally, since they read the same data
choices.why: Same data, different comparisons: a chosen number against a history.

choices.text: Neither, until the invoice arrives
choices.why: Both read daily cost data, well before an invoice.

choices.text: The budget, which compares the month with a number
choices.why: Right. It compares the month with a number somebody chose, and the steady cost adds up to it.

prompt: The shop buys a one-year reservation, paid up front, on 1 March. Its March chart shows a huge spike on day 1 and its February chart none. Which cost view would make the two months comparable?
hint: One view puts the purchase on the day it was paid.

choices.text: Amortised cost, which spreads the purchase
choices.why: Right. It spreads the purchase over the days it covers and charges each day's share to the resources.

choices.text: Actual cost, with the reservation filtered out
choices.why: Then March looks cheaper than it was: the machines covered by the reservation would seem free.

choices.text: Actual cost, grouped by resource
choices.why: Actual cost is the view that put the whole year on 1 March.

choices.text: Any view, as long as the granularity is monthly
choices.why: Monthly granularity still puts the whole purchase in March.

prompt: Budgets evaluate ___ cost, the cost as it was charged, not spread over time.
hint: The opposite of amortised.

prompt: Which of these are true of an Azure budget? Choose all that apply.
hint: Think about what it watches, how often, and what it can do.

choices.text: It can be written in Bicep and compiled with no account
choices.why: Right. `budget.bicep` compiled in the lab.

choices.text: It is evaluated as each charge arrives
choices.why: Once every 24 hours, against data that is itself hours late.

choices.text: It takes up to five notifications, each with its own threshold
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: It refuses new resources once the amount is passed
choices.why: It refuses nothing; it notifies.

choices.text: It can have actual and forecasted thresholds together
choices.why: Right, and the shop's has one of each.

prompt: A team sets one budget alert: actual cost at 100%. What does the lesson say they have given up?
hint: What does an actual alert at 100% tell you, and when?

choices.text: Nothing, since 100% of actual is the only alert that matters
choices.why: It matters, and it arrives after the whole amount is already spent.

choices.text: Any warning in time to act before the amount is spent
choices.why: Right. Only a forecast, or a lower actual threshold, speaks while there is time.

choices.text: The right to call an action group
choices.why: An action group can hang off any notification, actual ones included.

choices.text: Being notified by e-mail
choices.why: Every notification has its e-mail addresses; this one too.

prompt: Which tool would have caught `'Forecast'` in each file before Azure saw it?
hint: The lesson tried it in both.

choices.text: Bicep for the `.bicep` file, Terraform for `main.tf`
choices.why: Bicep compiled the misspelt value without a word.

choices.text: Neither tool: only Azure checks values
choices.why: Terraform's provider checked this value and refused it.

choices.text: Only Terraform, in `main.tf`
choices.why: Right. The `.bicep` copy went through to a template.

choices.text: Both, since both know the API's allowed values
choices.why: Bicep's types for this property list no allowed values.
